newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britons flock to Macau as visa deadline nears.
newsitem.headline: Britons flock to Macau as visa deadline nears.

text.p: Britons living in Hong Kong flocked to the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macau during the last Easter under British rule to make the most of one of their privileges before the colony is handed back to China.
Ferries making the hour-long trip to Macau were jammed, not only with Hong Kong Chinese heading for Macau's casinos but also with Britons, ferry operators and hotel managers said.
At present British passport-holders entering the colony automatically receive a 12-month visa allowing them to live and work in Hong Kong.
That privilege disappears this week as another chapter of colonial history ends in the run-up to Hong Kong's return to China at midnight on June 30.
From April 1 most British arrivals will receive a six-month non-working visa and those wanting to work in Hong Kong will have to apply for a permit.
So, for Britons an Easter trip to Macau and back means another 12-month visa in their passports.
The present British community includes many back-packers and students who have been able to pick up jobs, often in bars and restaurants catering for expatriates, after arriving in Hong Kong.
In future if people want to work, study or settle in Hong Kong, they will have to obtain a visa in the same way as other foreigners and the same criteria for approval will apply.
British citizens who have lived in Hong Kong for seven years and acquired the right to land can continue to enter and remain in Hong Kong without any restrictions.
Those who have been here less than seven years will be allowed to stay until their current limit of stay expires.

The last "British" Easter in Hong Kong, where about 500,000 of the 6.4 million people are Christians, highlighted concerns about religious freedom in the territory when it comes under communist Chinese rule.
China has pledged to maintain religious freedom, along with other rights enjoyed in capitalist Hong Kong under a concept called "One country, two systems".
But many people, particularly pro-democracy activists, doubt Beijing's word.
Hong Kong Catholic Bishop Joseph Zen said this month that people feared manipulation of the local church by Beijing.

"But basically we can believe that the concept of 'one country, two systems' is a sincere effort to keep Hong Kong as it is," Zen said in an interview published in the Sunday Examiner, a church publication.

"I am afraid that there may be cases in which they (Beijing) don't understand our system and then, without any conspiracy, they will intervene without knowing that they are damaging the Hong Kong system."
He said the Catholic church would hold a "very solemn" mass to mark Hong Kong's handover to China, but no big event to mark the start of a new era in Hong Kong's history.
